summary: A monarchy occupying most of the Arabian Peninsula, the birthplace of Islam, home to the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, and among the world leaders in oil reserves and production.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: Islam was founded in the 7th century by the Prophet Muhammad in Mecca and Medina, making the Arabian Peninsula the birthplace of Islam, and the two holy cities still draw Muslims from around the world on pilgrimage. In 1744 Muhammad ibn Saud of Diriyah allied with the religious scholar Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab to promote strict Wahhabi Sunni doctrine, and the Saudi state has been founded on it ever since. The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia was established in 1932, Islamic law is the basic law of the state, and citizens are legally required to be Muslim.

ranking.name: Islam (Shia)
ranking.description: Shia Muslims are mainly concentrated in the Eastern Province, especially Qatif and the Al-Ahsa oasis, where the Shia community has a long history going back to the early days of Islam. After the House of Saud conquered the east in 1913, the Shia long stood on the margins of a state dominated by Wahhabism. Shia protests occurred after the Iranian Revolution of 1979, and demonstrations also appeared in the east during the Arab Spring of 2011. In the southern region of Najran there is also an Ismaili community.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Christians are almost all foreign workers, mainly from the Philippines, India, Lebanon and Western countries, who came in large numbers after oil was discovered in 1938 and the oil economy took off in the 1970s. Saudi Arabia does not allow non-Islamic religious services to be held publicly or churches to be built, so believers can only worship in private places.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: Hindus are mainly foreign workers from India and Nepal, working in construction, healthcare and services. Because Saudi Arabia prohibits public non-Islamic religious activity, they can only practice their religion in private places.

religion.background: Before the founding of Islam the Arabian Peninsula had polytheistic beliefs, and the Kaaba in Mecca was a center of pilgrimage. In the 7th century Muhammad founded Islam, and Arab armies spread it around the world. In the 18th century Ibn Saud allied with al-Wahhab to establish a state centered on strict Sunni doctrine. The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia was founded in 1932, and the oil economy brought large numbers of foreign workers. Since 2016 'Vision 2030' has promoted social reform and the powers of the religious police have been reduced, but Islam remains the foundation of the state.

ranking.name: Arabic
ranking.description: Arabic is the language of the Quran, originating in the Arabian Peninsula, and after the founding of Islam in the 7th century it spread across the Middle East and North Africa with the Arab conquests. Saudi citizens almost all speak Arabic as their mother tongue, with local dialects including Najdi, Hejazi and Gulf dialects. Because the foreign population makes up about forty percent, Arabic speakers make up about eighty percent.

ranking.name: Hindustani (Urdu, Hindi)
ranking.description: Urdu and Hindi are the languages most used by South Asian foreign workers, and the two are close in spoken form. After the oil boom of the 1970s, large numbers of Pakistani and Indian workers came to Saudi Arabia to do construction, service and technical work, and they are among the largest groups of foreign workers in Saudi Arabia.

ranking.name: Bengali
ranking.description: Bengali is spoken by Bangladeshi foreign workers; Saudi Arabia is one of the main destinations of Bangladeshi overseas workers, who work mainly in construction, cleaning and agriculture, and remittances are an important pillar of the Bangladeshi economy.

ranking.name: Tagalog
ranking.description: Tagalog is spoken by foreign workers from the Philippines, who work in fields such as healthcare, nursing, domestic service, hotels and engineering. Since the 1970s the Philippine government has promoted the export of overseas workers, and Saudi Arabia has become one of the largest destinations of Filipino overseas workers.

language.history: Arabic was already the language of the Arabian Peninsula before the founding of Islam, and the pre-Islamic poetic tradition was very rich. The compilation of the Quran in the 7th century established the standard of Classical Arabic, and Islamic expansion made Arabic the language of scholarship and religion from Spain to Central Asia. Today Saudi Arabia uses Modern Standard Arabic as its official language, while local dialects are used in daily life. English is widely used in business and higher education.

ranking.name: Kabsa
ranking.description: Rice is cooked with tomato, onion, dried black lime and baharat spice blend, with chicken or lamb added, and served topped with almonds, raisins and fried onions.
ranking.history: Kabsa is a traditional dish of the Arabian Peninsula, and its name comes from the Arabic word for 'press', possibly related to the cooking method. The rice and spices mostly arrived through trade with India and Persia, while tomatoes became widespread only in the 20th century. Kabsa is regarded as Saudi Arabia's national dish, and at family gatherings, banquets and festivals people sit around one large tray and eat with the right hand, embodying Arab hospitality.

ranking.name: Mandi
ranking.description: Chicken or lamb marinated in spices is hung in a pit oven (taboon) and smoked, with the juices dripping onto the rice below, giving the rice a smoky aroma and the flavor of the meat juices.
ranking.history: Mandi originated in the Hadhramaut region of southern Yemen and was brought to Saudi Arabia by Hadhrami immigrants, being especially common in the Hejaz region, such as Jeddah and Mecca. The word 'mandi' comes from the Arabic word for 'dew', describing the moist texture of the meat. It is one of the most common dishes in Saudi restaurants and is often enjoyed at family weekend meals.

ranking.name: Mutabbaq (stuffed pancake)
ranking.description: Very thin dough is wrapped around minced meat, egg, and leek or scallion, folded into a square and fried on a large griddle until golden and crisp; there are also sweet versions filled with banana or cheese.
ranking.history: Mutabbaq derives from pan-fried dishes of India and Southeast Asia, brought to the Hejaz by Muslim traders and pilgrims from India and Southeast Asia, and the snack stalls of Jeddah and Mecca are especially famous for it. The name means 'folded' in Arabic, and from the Arabian Peninsula it spread again to Southeast Asia, where it is also very popular in Malaysia and Indonesia, reflecting culinary exchange along the pilgrimage routes.

ranking.name: Saleeg (milk rice)
ranking.description: Rice is cooked for a long time with chicken broth and milk, stirred into a thick, creamy milk rice and topped with roast chicken, with a mild taste, often enjoyed in winter and at family gatherings.
ranking.history: Saleeg is a traditional dish of Taif in the Hejaz region; Taif lies on a plateau with a cool climate and is a summer resort of the Hejaz. The dish is mild in taste and is considered suitable for the sick and for children. It is a common dish at family gatherings and weddings in the Hejaz, and is especially popular in the cold winter.

ranking.name: Arabic coffee (qahwa)
ranking.description: Lightly roasted coffee beans are ground and boiled with cardamom and saffron, poured into small handleless cups, and served to guests with dates, with a delicate flavor and the aroma of spices.
ranking.history: Coffee reached the Arabian Peninsula from Yemen in the 15th century, and Sufi monks were the first to drink it to stay awake during night prayers. In Saudi Arabia, serving Arabic coffee to guests is the most important rule of hospitality: the host pours the coffee from the pot with the right hand, and the guest shakes the cup to signal that no more is wanted. In 2015 UNESCO inscribed Arabic coffee on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and the Saudi government also designated 2022 the 'Year of Saudi Coffee'.
